name: Wireframe 3D
basis: 3D terrain from brightness, rotated and projected with the painter's algorithm (how)

lumenary.blurb: Brightness becomes terrain. Drag across it, or let it turn on its own.

facts.from: Early computer graphics and radio astronomy plots
facts.bestOn: Pictures with a bright subject on a dark ground

why: If brightness is read as altitude, a picture becomes a landscape, and a few hundred lines are enough to show it. This treatment builds that landscape and then does by hand what a 3D engine does: it rotates, tilts and projects it. Drawing the lines from back to front and filling under each one hides what is behind it, so ridges appear to stand in front of each other.
how: Sample the picture onto a grid and blur it lightly.
Turn every grid point into a 3D point whose height is its brightness.
Rotate it about the vertical axis, following your cursor or turning on its own, then tilt it towards the camera.
Project the points with perspective so nearer ones are drawn larger.
Draw lines from back to front, filling under each with the background colour so closer ridges hide farther ones.
history: Interactive 3D graphics began with Ivan Sutherland’s work in the 1960s, and the wireframe style defined early games such as Elite in 1984. The hidden-line trick used here is the painter’s algorithm, formalised in the early 1970s. Stacked ridge plots became famous through the 1979 Joy Division album Unknown Pleasures, whose cover reproduces a plot of pulsar pulses first drawn by Harold Craft in his 1970 thesis.
terms: Mapping 3D points to a flat screen so that distant things look smaller.
Drawing from the farthest thing to the nearest so that nearer things cover the rest.
Turning left or right, and tilting up or down.
paragraphs: Brightness is read as altitude. The picture is sampled onto a grid (up to 170 columns by the chosen number of lines), lightly blurred, and every grid point becomes a 3D point whose height is its brightness. The program then does what a 3D engine does, by hand: rotate the terrain about the vertical axis (the yaw, which follows your cursor or turns by itself), tilt it toward the camera (the pitch), and project it onto the screen with perspective, so that nearer points are drawn larger.

In ridgeline mode there is no depth buffer. Instead the lines are drawn from the back of the terrain to the front, and each line is first filled with the background colour below it. A closer ridge therefore hides the lines behind it, which is the painter’s algorithm and the way the famous pulsar album cover was drawn. Line opacity and thickness increase toward the front for a sense of depth. Mesh mode skips the fill and draws both rows and columns.

equations.note: Yaw ψ about the vertical axis, then pitch φ. (x, y, z) is the terrain point, with y = height × brightness.
Perspective projection from a camera at distance D; points with larger Z′ (nearer) get a larger scale s.

presets.text: Mesh mode draws both rows and columns, like a net over the picture.
Tall relief seen from a low camera makes a dramatic skyline.
Switch off the auto turn and drag across it by hand.
